facts.text: MSHA reported that powered haulage caused 13 of 33 US mining fatalities (39%) in calendar 2025.
facts.quote: in calendar 2025 powered haulage caused 13 of 33 mining fatalities (39%)

facts.text: MSHA reported that powered haulage caused 426 of 4,792 US mining nonfatal injuries (9%) in calendar 2025.
MSHA's Powered Haulage Safety page describes powered-haulage equipment as including shuttle cars, locomotives and front end loaders.
facts.quote: involving equipment "such as shuttle cars, locomotives, front end loaders and more" [1]

facts.text: At the 19 December 2023 final-rule announcement, MSHA counted 40 US mining deaths in 2023; this was a year-to-date count, not a final calendar-year total.
facts.quote: MSHA counted 40 mining deaths in 2023 (a year-to-date count at that date, not a final calendar-year total)

facts.text: Of the 40 US mining deaths counted by MSHA at the 19 December 2023 final-rule announcement, 16 were classified as machinery deaths and 10 as powered-haulage deaths.
facts.quote: 16 classified as machinery and 10 as powered haulage [31]

facts.text: MSHA identified 109 fatalities and 1,543 nonfatal injuries involving surface mobile equipment at mines with six or more miners from January 2003 to December 2018.
facts.quote: From January 2003 to December 2018 MSHA identified 109 fatalities and 1,543 nonfatal injuries involving surface mobile equipment at mines with six or more miners

facts.text: MSHA identified 10 surface-mobile-equipment fatalities at mines with five or fewer miners between 2013 and 2018.
facts.quote: mines with five or fewer miners had 10 such fatalities between 2013 and 2018 [32]

facts.text: The final rule on written safety programs for surface mobile equipment was published on 20 December 2023 and became effective on 19 January 2024.
facts.quote: The final rule on written safety programs for surface mobile equipment (published 20 December 2023, effective 19 January 2024)

entities.name: MSHA final rule on written safety programs for surface mobile equipment

facts.text: The final rule on written safety programs for surface mobile equipment cites 113 surface-mobile-equipment fatalities over a 10-year period; the passage labels the rule text Independent and the summary Vendor.
facts.quote: cites 113 surface mobile equipment fatalities over a 10-year period [33, 34, 35]. **Independent** (rule text) and **Vendor** (summary).

entities.name: MSHA final rule on written safety programs for surface mobile equipment

facts.text: NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672 (Ruff, 2007), based on MSHA fatality reports from 2000 to mid-2006, counted 22 fatalities involving blind areas.
facts.quote: NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672 (Ruff, 2007), based on MSHA fatality reports from 2000 to mid-2006, counted 22 fatalities involving blind areas.

facts.text: In NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672 (Ruff, 2007), dump trucks accounted for the highest share of fatal blind-area accidents (38%), followed by front-end loaders (33%).
facts.quote: "Equipment types with the highest number of fatal accidents were dump trucks (38%) followed by front-end loaders (33%)"

facts.text: NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672 (Ruff, 2007) reported that 67% of victims in fatal blind-area accidents were in the rear blind area of reversing equipment.
facts.quote: 67% of victims were "in the rear blind area of reversing equipment"

facts.text: Fatal blind-area accidents described in NIOSH Report of Investigations 9672 (Ruff, 2007) frequently involved large dump trucks driving over a smaller vehicle or a worker in a blind spot.
facts.quote: These accidents "frequently involved large dump trucks that drove over a smaller vehicle... or a worker who was in a blind spot" [2]

facts.text: Ruff's 2006 peer-reviewed companion paper in Accident Analysis & Prevention reported an average of five blind-area fatalities per year at US surface mines and quarries during 1999–2003.
facts.quote: The peer-reviewed companion paper (Ruff, 2006, Accident Analysis & Prevention) reported an average of five such fatalities a year at US surface mines and quarries during 1999 to 2003

facts.text: Ruff's 2006 paper in Accident Analysis & Prevention reported that blind-area fatalities represented 12% of all fatalities at US surface mines and quarries during 1999–2003.
facts.quote: 12% of all fatalities at those operations

facts.text: Ruff's 2006 paper in Accident Analysis & Prevention reported that dump trucks made up 58% of equipment involved in blind-area fatal accidents at US surface mines and quarries during 1999–2003.
facts.quote: with dump trucks making up 58% of the equipment involved [3]

facts.text: NIOSH estimated in 2000 that an average of 13 mine workers per year were killed by being run over or pinned by mobile mining equipment.
facts.quote: NIOSH estimated in 2000 that an average of 13 mine workers a year were killed by being run over or pinned by mobile mining equipment [36]

facts.text: The historical NIOSH and Ruff accident data predate current camera, radar and collision-avoidance technology and should not be interpreted as a 2026 fatality rate.
facts.quote: These data predate current camera, radar and collision-avoidance technology and should not be read as a 2026 rate

facts.text: The historical NIOSH and Ruff accident data confirm a persistent combination of very large blind zones and severe size mismatch in mobile mining equipment accidents.
facts.quote: they confirm the persistent combination of very large blind zones and severe size mismatch. **Independent**.
